healthcareSystem: Mixed public/private. Public hospitals (hospitales públicos) provide free care to everyone including tourists. Private health insurance (prepagas) offers faster, higher-quality care.
qualityNotes: Public hospitals in Buenos Aires and major cities offer good care and are free for tourists, but expect bureaucracy and long wait times. Private clinics are excellent, faster, and affordable by US standards. Many doctors speak English. Pharmacies (farmacias) are widely available.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 8am-10pm; some 24-hour pharmacies; chains include Farmacity, Dismerca, and regional chains; on-call (de turno) pharmacies listed in newspapers and online
pharmacyTips: Many common medications available OTC. Pharmacists are helpful. Bring a list with generic names. Some US OTC medications may not be available — bring your preferred brands. Pharmacias often have a 'pharmacy on call' system for nights/holidays.
prescriptionRules: A prescription is required for most prescription medications. Antibiotics and many drugs are available OTC with less strict enforcement than in the US. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note in Spanish or English.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances in Argentina. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare to customs. A local prescription may be needed for larger quantities.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Some codeine products require prescription. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Bring a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

restrictedMeds.name: Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta)
restrictedMeds.note: Bring documentation and only the amount needed for your stay.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in Spanish or English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Spanish translations are helpful.

travelInsurance.tips: Public hospitals are free but can be slow and bureaucratic. Private healthcare is affordable ($50-150/doctor visit, $300-1,000/day hospital stay) but still requires payment. Travel insurance with medical coverage and evacuation is strongly recommended. Consider coverage for adventure activities (Patagonia trekking, mountaineering) if applicable.

recommended: Yellow Fever (recommended for travel to Iguazú Falls area and Northern provinces; required for some national parks)
vaccinations.notes: No required vaccinations for most travelers. Yellow fever vaccination is recommended for travel to northern provinces and Iguazú Falls region. Check specific requirements if visiting national parks in Patagonia. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

waterNotes: Tap water is generally safe to drink in Buenos Aires and major cities. In rural areas and smaller towns, bottled water is recommended. In Patagonia (especially rural areas), follow local advisories. Bottled water is widely available everywhere.
foodSafetyTips: Argentina has excellent food safety standards in restaurants and hotels. Asado (Argentine BBQ) is safe at reputable restaurants. Be cautious with street food in informal areas. In Patagonia, stick to well-cooked meats. Empanadas from reputable vendors are generally safe. Dairy products (especially raw cheese) in rural areas should be approached with caution.
medicalTourismNote: Argentina is a popular medical tourism destination, particularly for cosmetic surgery, dental work, and fertility treatments. Costs are 50-80% lower than in the US and Western Europe. Buenos Aires is the main hub. Many doctors are trained in Europe or the US. JCI-accredited hospitals available.
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Argentina. Emergency numbers (107/101/911), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, vaccination requirements, and travel insurance advice.

hospitals.name: Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires
hospitals.notes: Argentina's top-rated hospital. International patient department.

hospitals.name: Hospital Alemán
hospitals.notes: Private hospital in the tourist-friendly Recoleta neighborhood.

pharmacyPhrases.english: I need medicine for a headache
pharmacyPhrases.local: Necesito medicamento para el dolor de cabeza

dentalCare.availability: Good dental care at affordable prices. Buenos Aires is a dental tourism destination.
dentalCare.notes: Quality is good in Buenos Aires. Argentina is increasingly popular for dental tourism due to favorable exchange rates.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: Hospital emergency departments handle dental emergencies. Pharmacies can provide pain relief.

mentalHealth.internationalLine: Buenos Aires has a strong psychotherapy culture — therapists widely available.
mentalHealth.englishTherapists: Available in Buenos Aires, especially in Palermo and Recoleta neighborhoods.
mentalHealth.notes: Argentina has the highest number of psychologists per capita in the world. Finding an English-speaking therapist in Buenos Aires is relatively easy.

accessibilityInfo.overview: Buenos Aires has been improving accessibility. Newer buses are low-floor. Sidewalks in older neighborhoods can be uneven.
accessibilityInfo.transport: Subte (metro) has limited accessibility. Colectivos (buses) are increasingly accessible. Taxis are the most flexible option.
accessibilityInfo.tips: San Telmo cobblestones and La Boca sidewalks can be challenging. Puerto Madero is the most accessible neighborhood.

insuranceClaimProcess: Public hospitals (hospitales públicos) provide free emergency care to everyone, including tourists. Private hospitals require payment or insurance. Keep all facturas and medical reports. Request English documentation.

commonCosts.note: Estimated typical out-of-pocket costs at private or international facilities. Public-system rates can be much lower (or free for residents). Actual costs vary by city, facility, and exchange rate.

medicalEvacuation.note: Local hospitals handle the vast majority of cases — air evacuation is rarely needed for tourists. If a condition exceeds local capacity: São Paulo (Hospital Albert Einstein, Sírio-Libanês) is the leading South American medical hub. Buenos Aires and Santiago handle southern-cone cases.
